newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU's Cresson rules out human cloning research.
newsitem.headline: EU's Cresson rules out human cloning research.

text.p: The European Union opposes research into human cloning, EU Research Commissioner Edith Cresson said on Tuesday.
"For obvious ethical reasons, there is a consensus among the international scientific community to ban research into human cloning," Cresson told the European Parliament.
Cresson, a former French socialist prime minister, noted that EU research programmes excluded human cloning and several member states had also banned such work.

Reacting to the recent successful cloning of a sheep, named Dolly, at Scotland's Roslin Institute, Cresson said this raised important ethical questions about animal welfare, biodiversity and possible risks of extending such techniques to humans.
Cresson said the EU's executive commission had asked its biotechnology ethics committee, an independent advisory body, to report back on the implications of the Scottish cloning by May.

The most obvious danger was the temptation to use the technique, which creates genetically identical individuals by splitting embryos or by transferring the nucleus of one cell into an egg, to clone humans.
"But we should not underestimate potential benefits of such a discovery, notably for human health," Cresson said.
Advocates of animal cloning point to other advantages, such as the possibility of producing sheep which are entirely free from scrapie, a disease similar to mad cow disease.
"There are ethical problems in using the technique. There are ethical problems in not using the techniques as well," said Ken Collins, chairman of the parliament's environment committee.
Euro-MPs from across the political spectrum ruled out taking the technique further and cloning human beings.
They are expected on Wednesday to pass a resolution demanding an immediate global ban on human cloning and a moratorium on animal cloning.
"We cannot assume that because we have something under control in the European Union, that it is universally under control. It isn't," Collins warned.

Euro-MPs want the Commission to play a leading role in pushing for a worldwide ban on human cloning, namely by convincing Japan and the United States -- the EU's main competitors in the field of biotechnology.
